gaps.sentence: He has lived in Berlin and Prague, and loves ___ cities.
gaps.explanation: 'Both cities' refers to the two cities mentioned; 'all' would suggest three or more.

gaps.sentence: ___ time I visit Rome, I discover something new.
gaps.explanation: 'Every time I ...' introduces repeated occasions; 'all time' and 'whole time' are not used here.

gaps.sentence: Does the project need ___ more work?
gaps.explanation: 'Work' is uncountable here, so 'much more work' is correct; 'many more work' is impossible.

gaps.sentence: We had ___ luggage that the taxi couldn't take it all.
gaps.explanation: 'So much luggage that …' — luggage is uncountable.

gaps.sentence: She has two children. One lives in Leeds, and ___ lives in York.
gaps.hint: one of a pair of two
gaps.explanation: 'One ... the other ...' is the pattern for exactly two; 'another' would imply more than two.

gaps.sentence: He isn't old ___ to drive a car.
gaps.explanation: 'Old enough' means sufficiently old; 'enough' follows the adjective, while 'too' gives the opposite meaning.

gaps.sentence: If you walk instead of driving, you'll spend ___ on petrol.
gaps.explanation: 'Spend less' is the comparative with uncountable money; 'fewer' is for countable nouns.

gaps.sentence: We had five applications, but ___ of the candidates was suitable.
gaps.hint: more than two candidates + singular verb
gaps.explanation: 'None of the candidates was ...' is used for three or more; 'neither' is reserved for two.
